title: Unicorns in the Making: The Strategy Behind Hypergrowth
description: A conversation about priorities, hiring, products and international growth at fast-growing AI companies. Moderator: Amanda Perran.

summary.overview: Growth can create a new problem for a successful technology startup: the habits that helped it find its first customers may no longer work when hundreds of people are involved. At techNL Summit, CoLab’s Taylor Young and Spellbook’s Chris Gardner discussed how their companies have changed priorities, product-development decisions, management and hiring as they have scaled. Both argued that companies must learn which work actually advances the business, distinguish customer problems from customers’ preferred solutions and repeatedly redesign responsibilities. Their clearest shared constraint was talent: hiring people who can operate independently amid uncertainty takes longer than either would like.

keyTakeaways.heading: Focus changes as the company earns room to expand
keyTakeaways.explanation: Young said CoLab initially concentrated on a narrow manufacturing market and a limited set of engineering collaboration problems. That discipline made it possible to gain traction before pursuing broader opportunities. At scale, the challenge reverses: leaders have to recognize when saying yes to new products or markets serves a longer-term strategy rather than distracting from it.

keyTakeaways.heading: Customer problems matter more than requested features
keyTakeaways.explanation: Gardner recalled how Spellbook’s earlier product followed what legal teams described wanting but failed to gain meaningful use. An AI-first approach provided a different way to solve the underlying problem. Young similarly distinguished between enterprise buyers and the engineers who use CoLab daily, noting that their needs and behaviour do not always align.

keyTakeaways.heading: Talent that thrives with ambiguity is a growth bottleneck
keyTakeaways.explanation: Both speakers said finding the right employees had become one of their biggest constraints. Young valued people who take ownership, act with limited supervision, learn quickly and accept changing responsibilities. He also stressed that the required balance of specialist experience and transferable soft skills differs by role.

detailedSummary.heading: A narrow beginning gives a company the right to expand
paragraphs: Young described CoLab’s original focus on the communication difficulties of engineers collaborating on complex mechanical designs. Rather than trying to serve every manufacturing market at once, the company concentrated on a comparatively narrow group of industrial equipment customers and use cases. His argument was that an early company needs to be disciplined enough to reject many attractive opportunities.

As the business grows, however, doing only what worked in the first years may limit its future. Young said new product and market choices should be assessed against a five- or ten-year vision, then worked backward to decide what belongs in the next phase. Gardner similarly warned against spending attention on small, satisfying fires that do not help win customers or advance the business.

detailedSummary.heading: Build around the customer’s problem, then watch actual use
paragraphs: Gardner explained that Spellbook’s earlier incarnation spent time inside a law firm and built the workflow lawyers requested. The resulting product did not see the expected adoption. The team later shifted toward an AI-first contract product, which addressed the underlying work in a way customers had not necessarily known to request.

Young agreed that customers are good at describing problems but may not be able to prescribe the best solution. CoLab’s challenge is complicated by large-enterprise buying: the executive approving a purchase can be far removed from the individual engineer using the software. Both speakers emphasized putting usable products in front of customers and learning from behaviour, not just verbal endorsements.

detailedSummary.heading: AI has changed the economics of experimentation
paragraphs: Gardner described much faster feature development with AI-assisted engineering, including an example of work once scheduled far into the roadmap being prototyped much sooner. He also pointed out that the savings in developer time do not eliminate costs such as model or token usage.

Young said cheaper, faster implementation encourages his team to test more ideas directly. Where a six-month project once allowed months of discussion before release, a much shorter development cycle changes how product teams collect evidence. The result is not that validation disappears, but that working experiments can play a larger part in discovery.

detailedSummary.heading: What breaks when headcount grows
paragraphs: The panellists identified shared decision-making and ambiguous ownership as growing pains. In a small team, nearly everyone can be involved in important discussions and feel responsible for the whole company. With hundreds of employees, that approach slows decisions and leaves accountability unclear.

Young argued that leaders must create room for others to own decisions, make mistakes and learn, even when the founder believes they know how to do the work themselves. He described repeatedly handing responsibilities to new specialists and then moving into the next unfamiliar challenge. Gardner described similarly changing roles and hierarchies as Spellbook expanded. Both cautioned against assuming that a fast-growing company has tidy, settled processes behind its public success.

detailedSummary.heading: Hiring for stretch, self-direction and the changing role
paragraphs: Asked directly what makes a strong new hire, Gardner emphasized tolerance for chaos, comfort with ambiguity and the ability to take a clearly defined outcome and drive it with little supervision. Young agreed on the importance of independent ownership but made a distinction between roles: some functions have established training processes and rely heavily on soft skills, while others still require rare combinations of domain expertise, startup experience and personal initiative.

Young said CoLab has had notable success hiring people into stretch roles—individuals who had not performed the exact position or operated at the same scale before, but were eager to learn and willing to work directly on hard problems. He contrasted this with the risk of bringing in an experienced leader who expects to manage from a distance rather than get involved. Both speakers described recruiting as slow and difficult because candidates also have to want the uncertainty of a high-growth environment.

highlightedInsight.heading: Ownership cannot scale unless leaders actually hand it over
highlightedInsight.explanation: Young’s distinction was not simply that startups need proactive employees. He argued that leaders must allow those people to exercise judgment, make mistakes and own outcomes. Otherwise, the very behaviour the organization wants to hire for is constrained by its management habits.

notableIdeas: CoLab’s narrow early market focus on industrial equipment made a later expansion of its product strategy more deliberate.
Young said staying in direct contact with customers is one responsibility leaders should resist delegating entirely, because otherwise their decisions can rely on stale market information.
Both speakers described job descriptions and responsibilities as fluid at high-growth companies: work may be handed off, reclaimed during a transition and redefined again.
Gardner described unrestricted AI access as both a productivity enabler and an expense-management challenge; his anecdotal figures are not presented as audited company costs.
practicalApplications: For candidates: prepare an example of a project you advanced without detailed instructions, including the decisions you made and how you validated the result.

For hiring managers: separate roles with teachable workflows from positions requiring a rare technical or domain background, and evaluate ownership rather than treating previous titles as the only signal.
For product teams: ask customers what problem they are trying to solve, put a working solution in front of users and measure what they actually do.
For growing leaders: revisit responsibilities and delegation regularly so that decisions do not become bottlenecked around the people who previously owned everything.
